1.e4 c5 2.b4.name: Sicilian Defence: Wing Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.b4.background: Generally considered too reckless, it is rarely seen in grandmaster play. In 1994 Joe Gallagher called it “a forgotten relic, hardly having set foot in a tournament hall since the days of Frank Marshall and Rudolph Spielmann”.

1.e4 c5 2.b4 cxb4.strategy: Accepting is sound: Black is a pawn up and the c-pawn has left the centre, which was the point of the gambit. White must show enough for the pawn in a quick central build-up, and the gambit rarely does.

1.e4 c5 2.b4 d5.strategy: Declines the gambit and strikes at e4 at once, so the b-pawn move has done nothing for White. After the exchange on d5 the recapturing queen can be hit by Nc3 and the pawn on c5 stays under attack, so Black must play accurately.

1.e4 c5 2.b4 e6.strategy: Ignores the gambit and develops: if White takes on c5, the bishop recaptures and material is level. The b-pawn has then gone for nothing, but Black gives up the extra pawn that accepting would bring in exchange for a simple, safe game.

1.e4 c5 2.b4 cxb4 3.a3.name: Sicilian Defence: Wing Gambit, Marshall Variation
1.e4 c5 2.b4 cxb4 3.a3.strategy: Attacks the advanced pawn at once: if Black takes again, White recaptures with a piece and gets quick development and open queenside files for the pawns; if not, axb4 deflects Black's c-pawn and prepares a central pawn break. It is the usual way to play the gambit, but the second pawn does not come for free.

1.e4 c5 2.b4 cxb4 3.Bb2.name: Sicilian Defence: Wing Gambit, Abrahams Variation
1.e4 c5 2.b4 cxb4 3.Bb2.strategy: Develops the bishop straight onto the long diagonal, where it presses on g7, and leaves the pawn on b4 alone for now. Black simply keeps the extra pawn and has no weakness yet, so White is left to show that quick development is worth a pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.b4 cxb4 3.c4.name: Sicilian Defence: Wing Gambit, Santasiere Variation
1.e4 c5 2.b4 cxb4 3.c4.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn pair on c4 and e4 but does nothing about the pawn on b4. Black can keep it, or take en passant on c3 to thin out White's queenside; either way White is still a pawn down and must justify it by development alone.

1.e4 c5 2.b4 cxb4 3.a3 d5.strategy: The antidote: instead of taking more material, Black counterattacks in the centre. The e4 pawn is attacked and nothing defends it, and 4.axb4 would lose it to ...dxe4. Black keeps the extra pawn and gains the centre, and White's compensation is hard to find.

1.e4 c5 2.b4 cxb4 3.a3 bxa3.name: Sicilian Defence: Wing Gambit, Carlsbad Variation
1.e4 c5 2.b4 cxb4 3.a3 bxa3.strategy: Grabs a second pawn, the greedy way to meet the gambit. White recaptures with a piece and gets what the gambit was played for: quick development and open files on the queenside, against Black's extra material and a king's side still to be developed.

1.e4 c5 2.b4 cxb4 3.a3 e6.strategy: A solid second choice: the e-pawn opens the bishop's diagonal, so that a recapture on b4 is answered by ...Bxb4 and Black keeps the extra pawn. But it leaves the e4 pawn alone, which lets White build a centre and use the time to develop.

1.e4 c5 2.b4 cxb4 3.a3 d5 4.exd5.strategy: Takes first instead of defending e4, trading the attacked pawn for Black's d-pawn. It is the cleanest answer to the counterattack, but the black queen recaptures into the centre, so White's lead in development now has to do the work of the missing pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.b4 cxb4 3.a3 d5 4.e5.strategy: Avoids the exchange and closes the centre: the pawn on e5 gains space, cannot be taken, and leaves Black's d-pawn in place. White is still a pawn down and has to make development and the queenside files count, while Black strikes at the new pawn chain with pieces at once.

1.e4 c5 2.b4 cxb4 3.a3 d5 4.axb4.strategy: Takes the gambit pawn back, but the e4 pawn is still attacked and nothing defends it: ...dxe4 wins it, and White is again a pawn down, with an open a-file as the only return for a central pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.b4 cxb4 3.a3 d5 4.exd5 Qxd5.strategy: Recaptures with the queen, which stands well in the centre and eyes g2. It also sets a trap: the greedy 5.axb4?? runs into ...Qe5+, a check that attacks the rook on a1 and wins it.

1.e4 c5 2.b4 cxb4 3.a3 d5 4.exd5 Nf6.strategy: Attacks the d5 pawn with a developing move instead of recapturing with the queen. After axb4 and ...Nxd5 material is level, so Black hands back the gambit pawn for a quick development and a queen that stays at home.

1.e4 c5 2.b4 cxb4 3.a3 d5 4.exd5 bxa3.strategy: Takes a second gambit pawn before recapturing on d5. White regains it with a developing move and gets open queenside files and a lead in development, while Black is still a pawn up but has to bring the king's side out under pressure.

1.e4 c5 2.b4 cxb4 3.a3 d5 4.exd5 Qxd5 5..strategy: The right way to win the pawn back: White develops first. The knight covers e5, so Qe5+ stops being an answer and the threat of axb4 is real again. Black has to defend the pawn on b4 or give it back.

1.e4 c5 2.b4 cxb4 3.a3 d5 4.exd5 Qxd5 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Wing Gambit, Marienbad Variation
1.e4 c5 2.b4 cxb4 3.a3 d5 4.exd5 Qxd5 5..strategy: Puts the bishop on the long diagonal, so that axb4 no longer allows the queen check on e5: the bishop would take the queen. The price is that the bishop steps onto a square the b4 pawn can attack with ...bxa3, forcing White to recapture and remain a pawn down.

Covers the e-file, so Black's queen can no longer come to e5, where the white queen would take it, and the threat of axb4 is back. The queen blocks the king's bishop and develops nothing, and Black can defend b4 or take on a3 and stay a pawn up.

Takes the centre with a pawn and opens the diagonal for the king's bishop, which now defends the pawn on b4 and answers axb4 in kind. It also gains space and keeps ...e4 in hand to drive the knight away with a gain of time.

Defends the pawn on b4 with a developing move: if White takes with the a-pawn, the knight retakes and Black keeps the extra pawn. It commits to holding the queenside pawn rather than to taking the centre, so White gets time to build a lead in development.

Takes a second gambit pawn once more. White recaptures with a developing move, with open queenside files and a lead in development against Black's undeveloped king's side, and the queen in the centre is exposed to gains of time.

Attacks the queen with a pawn and wins a tempo, and takes control of d5. It also gives up the chance to cover d4 with a pawn, leaving a hole there for Black's pieces. White is still a pawn down and has to make the lead in development count.

Aims at the e5 pawn: the knight and the bishop both attack it and only the queen defends it, so Nxe5 is a real threat. It develops with a threat, but Black has natural ways to cover e5 and keeps the extra pawn.

Takes the gambit pawn back and opens the a-file. The pawn on e5 now blocks the queen from that square, so no check wins the rook as it did earlier. Black can retake with the bishop and stay a pawn up, but White drives it back with a gain of time and plays for development.

The natural defence: a developing move that gives e5 the second defender it needs, so that taking on e5 would just lose material. Black keeps the pawn on b4, the extra pawn and the centre, and White has to look for other compensation on the long diagonal.

Drives the knight away with a gain of time instead of defending e5. The pawn grabs space but stands advanced and without a neighbour, White's knight settles on an active square on d4, and Black still has to finish development.

Holds the e5 pawn with a pawn, which frees the queen from guard duty and keeps the extra pawn. It takes the natural square from the king's knight and loosens the king's position, so it is the least natural way to keep the pawn.

The queen steps out of the attack to a square from which it still guards the e5 pawn and eyes the c4 pawn. Black keeps the pawn up and the centre intact, while White can no longer cover d4 with a pawn.

Steps out of the attack to a square from which it guards both the e5 pawn and the pawn on b4, so a recapture on b4 can be met by the queen. It blocks the king's bishop, though, so Black's development is slower than with the queen on e6.

Checks and offers the queens off: after 7.Qe2 Qxe2+ the white lead in development counts for less and Black keeps the extra pawn. But White can interpose 7.Be2 and keep the queens on, and the queen on e4 is a target for gains of time.
